label: listing examples, any will do
meaning_en: A particle for naming examples of a kind, where any of them would do: “X or Y or the like, things such as X or Y”. It is the conversational sibling of “이라든지”.
usage: It attaches to nouns: “이라든가” after a final consonant, “라든가” after a vowel (“커피라든가”). It is usually repeated after each item and then followed by “하는” plus the category noun. The items are examples, not a closed choice. It is colloquial and sounds casual in writing.

examples.ko: 돈이라든가 학벌이라든가 하는 것은 별로 중요하지 않아.
examples.en: Things like money or educational background aren't that important.

examples.ko: 커피라든가 차라든가 마실 것을 좀 준비해 주세요.
examples.en: Please get something to drink, such as coffee or tea.

examples.ko: 주말에는 영화라든가 전시회라든가 문화생활을 즐기는 사람이 많다.
examples.en: On weekends many people enjoy cultural activities such as movies or exhibitions.

examples.ko: 사랑이라든가 우정이라든가 하는 말은 너무 흔해서 마음에 와닿지 않는다.
examples.en: Words like “love” or “friendship” are so common that they do not strike a chord.

examples.ko: 한국 음식이라든가 한국 노래라든가 이런저런 것에 관심이 생겼어요.
examples.en: I have become interested in all sorts of things, like Korean food or Korean songs.

compare.difference: “이나” offers a choice between the items; “이라든가” gives them as samples of a kind.

pair.en: Buy apples or pears (one of the two).

pair.ko: 사과라든가 배라든가 과일을 좀 사 오세요.
pair.en: Buy some fruit, such as apples or pears.

compare.difference: “이든지” says any item is fine; “이라든가” lists examples to describe a category.

pair.en: Coffee or tea, anything is fine, please.
Please give me something to drink, like coffee or tea.

pitfalls.note: After a noun that ends in a vowel the “이” drops.
pitfalls.en: Please give me something to drink, like coffee or tea.

topik_tip: In 읽기 passages the noun that follows “하는” after a “-라든가 … -라든가” list names the category the items illustrate.

label: unusually, today of all days
meaning_en: A particle that marks a particular day or time as different from the usual, for no clear reason: “just today, of all days, for some reason today”. What follows describes something out of the ordinary.
usage: It attaches without a space to time nouns, above all “오늘따라” and “그날따라”, and the clause that follows describes something unlike the usual, often an annoying or surprising thing. It is not used with people or things. It is a different word from the “에 따라” of “depending on”.

examples.ko: 오늘따라 길이 왜 이렇게 막히지?
examples.en: Why is the road so jammed today of all days?

examples.ko: 평소에는 잘 먹던 아이가 그날따라 밥을 한 숟가락도 먹지 않았다.
examples.en: The child, who normally eats well, did not eat a single spoonful that day.

examples.ko: 이상하게 오늘따라 네가 더 멋있어 보여.
examples.en: Strangely, you look cooler than usual today.

examples.ko: 그날따라 하늘이 유난히 맑고 푸르렀다.
examples.en: That day, for some reason, the sky was especially clear and blue.

examples.ko: 하필 오늘따라 우산을 안 가져왔네.
examples.en: Today of all days I didn't bring an umbrella.

compare.difference: “은/는” simply contrasts today with other days; “따라” says today is out of the ordinary.

pair.en: The road is jammed today, unlike usual.
The road is jammed today (as opposed to other days).

compare.difference: “유난히” stresses how great the degree is; “따라” stresses that this particular time is unlike the others.

pair.en: I'm tired today, unlike usual.
Today I am especially tired.

pitfalls.note: It is a particle, so it is written without a space.
pitfalls.en: The road is jammed today of all days.

label: even (the unlikeliest case)
meaning_en: A particle meaning “even”: it picks out the extreme or least expected case and says it is included too. It usually goes with a negative or unwelcome situation.
usage: It attaches to nouns and to nominalised verbs (“숨 쉬기조차”), and it also follows “에게”, “에서” and the like (“집에서조차”). It replaces “이/가” and “을/를”, so it is never followed by them; “조차도” is possible. Its predicate is most often negative (“없다”, “못 -”, “않다”), though a positive one is not forbidden.

examples.ko: 너무 바빠서 밥 먹을 시간조차 없었어요.
examples.en: I was so busy that I did not even have time to eat.

examples.ko: 그 사실은 가족조차 몰랐다.
examples.en: Even the family did not know that fact.

examples.ko: 이름조차 모르는 사람이 갑자기 연락을 해 왔다.
examples.en: Someone whose name I don't even know suddenly contacted me.

examples.ko: 숨 쉬기조차 힘들 만큼 가슴이 답답했다.
examples.en: My chest felt so tight that even breathing was hard.

examples.ko: 전문가조차 이번 결과는 예상하지 못했다.
examples.en: Even the experts did not foresee this result.

compare.difference: “도” just adds one more; “조차” says this is the case you would least expect.

pair.en: Even Seunggyu did not know that.
Seunggyu did not know that either.

compare.difference: “조차” stresses the most unexpected case; “마저” stresses that it is the last one left after the others were lost.

pair.en: Even my family, of all people, did not believe me.
Even my family, the last ones I had, did not believe me.

pitfalls.note: It replaces the subject and object particles; it does not stack on them.
pitfalls.en: I could not even drink water.

topik_tip: A clause with “조차” most often ends in “없다”, “못” or a negative form, which helps when choosing among “도”, “조차” and “마저”.

label: contrast: it's A, not B
meaning_en: A connective ending that states one fact and sets it against another, usually negated one: “it is A, not B; A is the case, but B is not”. It is how you correct or pin down a point.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems and to “이다” (“이지”, or “지” after a vowel), and it can follow “-었-”. The second clause is normally negative (“아니다”, “않다”, “못하다”) or a clear counterpoint. It is conversational and also appears in essays. This is the contrastive “-지”, not the sentence-final “-지” of confirmation.

examples.ko: 고래는 포유류이지 어류가 아니다.
examples.en: A whale is a mammal, not a fish.

examples.ko: 말이 쉽지 막상 하려면 얼마나 어려운데요.
examples.en: Saying it is easy, but actually doing it is hard.

examples.ko: 저는 도와 달라고 부탁하는 거지 대신 해 달라는 게 아닙니다.
examples.en: I am asking for your help, not asking you to do it for me.

examples.ko: 내가 화난 건 네가 거짓말을 해서지 약속에 늦어서가 아니야.
examples.en: I am angry because you lied, not because you were late.

examples.ko: 이번 사고는 개인의 실수이지 제도의 문제가 아니라는 입장이 나왔다.
examples.en: A view was voiced that this accident was an individual's mistake, not a problem with the system.

compare.difference: “-지만” just says “but”; “-지” sets up a correction, so the second clause usually denies or corrects.

pair.en: It's easy to say, but hard to do.
It is easy to say, but hard to do.

compare.difference: Both give the same facts; “-지” puts the true statement first, “이/가 아니라” puts the denial first.

pair.en: A whale is a mammal, not a fish.
A whale is not a fish but a mammal.

pitfalls.note: Two positive clauses cannot be set against each other with “-지”; the second one has to deny or correct.
pitfalls.right: 저는 커피를 마시지 차는 안 마셔요.
pitfalls.en: I drink coffee; I don't drink tea.

label: not only but also
meaning_en: A connective ending meaning “not only … but also …”: the first fact is real, and a second one of the same kind is added to it.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-을뿐더러”, or “-ㄹ뿐더러” after a vowel or ㄹ (“좁을뿐더러”, “들뿐더러”), to a noun with “일뿐더러”, and after “-었-”. It has no present form of its own, so “-는” is not used. It is written without a space and is rather formal or written. Both clauses should be on the same side, both good or both bad, and the second often carries “도” or “까지”.

examples.ko: 이 식당은 음식이 맛있을뿐더러 가격도 저렴하다.
examples.en: The food at this restaurant is delicious, and the prices are cheap too.

examples.ko: 운동은 건강에 좋을뿐더러 스트레스를 푸는 데에도 도움이 된다.
examples.en: Exercise is good for your health and also helps you relieve stress.

examples.ko: 그 길은 좁을뿐더러 가로등도 없어서 밤에는 위험하다.
examples.en: The road is narrow and has no streetlights either, so it is dangerous at night.

examples.ko: 이 일은 시간이 많이 들뿐더러 비용도 만만치 않다.
examples.en: This job takes a lot of time, and the cost is not small either.

examples.ko: 그분은 훌륭한 의사일뿐더러 존경받는 스승이기도 하다.
examples.en: That person is an excellent doctor and also a respected teacher.

compare.difference: Both add a second point. “-는 데다가” is more everyday; “-을뿐더러” is more formal and sounds written.

pair.en: The road is narrow, and dark as well.
The road is narrow, and on top of that dark.

compare.difference: They mean the same. “-을 뿐만 아니라” is the more common, neutral form and is written with a space; “-을뿐더러” is a single ending.

pair.en: It is tasty and cheap too.
It is not only tasty but also cheap.

pitfalls.note: It is a single ending, so there is no space before “뿐더러”.
pitfalls.wrong: 이 가게는 맛있을 뿐더러 값도 싸다.
pitfalls.en: This shop is tasty and cheap too.

pitfalls.note: The ending is “-을”, not the present “-는”.
pitfalls.en: This shop is tasty and cheap too.

topik_tip: It is a handy formal link in 쓰기 answers when you stack two reasons or merits; keep both on the same side, good with good or bad with bad.

label: repeated action, used to
meaning_en: A connective ending, mostly in “-고는 하다” and its contraction “-곤 하다”, meaning that an action happens again and again: “would often, used to, tend to”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems only, and the shortened form “-곤” is the usual one in speech and writing: “가곤 한다”, “가곤 했다”. Use it for repeated or habitual actions, in the present or the past; a single occurrence cannot take it. Adverbs such as “가끔”, “자주”, “종종” often go with it.

examples.ko: 어릴 때 우리는 방학마다 할머니 댁에 가곤 했다.
examples.en: When we were little, we would go to Grandmother's house every vacation.

examples.ko: 아버지는 퇴근길에 서점에 들르곤 하셨다.
examples.en: My father would stop by a bookstore on his way home from work.

examples.ko: 스트레스를 받으면 저는 혼자 노래방에 가곤 해요.
examples.en: When I'm stressed, I often go to a karaoke room alone.

examples.ko: 가끔 옛 친구들이 생각나곤 한다.
examples.en: Now and then I find myself thinking of old friends.

examples.ko: 비 오는 날이면 그 카페에 앉아 책을 읽곤 했다.
examples.en: On rainy days I would sit in that cafe and read.

compare.difference: “-ㄴ 적이 있다” says something has happened at least once; “-곤 하다” says it recurs.

pair.ko: 어릴 때 그 강에서 수영하곤 했다.
pair.en: I used to swim in that river when I was little.

pair.ko: 어릴 때 그 강에서 수영한 적이 있다.
pair.en: I have swum in that river when I was little.

compare.difference: “-는 편이다” describes a general tendency; “-곤 하다” points to an action that recurs from time to time.

pair.en: I sleep late on weekends from time to time.
I tend to sleep late on weekends.

pitfalls.note: A single past event cannot take it; the action has to repeat.
pitfalls.en: I met a friend yesterday.

label: because I saw/heard
meaning_en: A colloquial connective ending giving the reason or basis for what follows: “seeing/hearing that X, I did Y”. The first clause is something observed or heard, and the main clause is the speaker's own reaction or action.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems, to “이다” (“이길래”) and after “-었-”. Its first clause is usually about someone or something other than the speaker, and the main clause is usually in the past. It cannot be followed by a command or a suggestion. In questions it appears as “뭐길래”, “얼마나 -길래” (“what is it that…, how … must it be that…”).

examples.ko: 하늘이 흐리길래 우산을 챙겨 나왔어요.
examples.en: The sky was cloudy, so I took an umbrella with me.

examples.ko: 가게 앞에 사람들이 길게 줄을 서 있길래 무슨 일인가 싶어서 들어가 봤다.
examples.en: Seeing a long line of people in front of the shop, I wondered what was going on and went in.

examples.ko: 얼마나 맛있길래 다들 저렇게 줄을 서는 거야?
examples.en: How delicious must it be for everyone to line up like that?

examples.ko: 동생이 하도 졸라 대길래 결국 장난감을 사 주고 말았다.
examples.en: My younger sibling kept pestering me so much that I ended up buying the toy.

examples.ko: 도대체 무슨 소식이길래 다들 저렇게 놀라는 거예요?
examples.en: What on earth is the news that has everyone so shocked?

compare.difference: “-아서/어서” is a neutral reason; “-길래” presents something the speaker noticed and then reacted to.

pair.en: Seeing that it was snowing, I went out to look.
It snowed, so I went out to look.

compare.difference: “-기에” is the written or more formal counterpart; “-길래” is the spoken contraction.

pair.en: Seeing the dark look on their face, I asked.
Seeing the dark look on their face, I asked (more formal).

pitfalls.note: The cause should not be the speaker's own state.
pitfalls.en: I was hungry, so I ate.

pitfalls.note: It cannot be followed by a command or a suggestion.
pitfalls.en: It's cold, so please wear a coat.

label: if you keep doing, trouble
meaning_en: A connective ending with two uses. Its main use is a warning: “if you keep doing X, a bad result will follow”. It can also mean that one action or state stops and shifts to another: “X for a while, and then Y”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems (“-다간” in speech). In the warning use, the main clause predicts a negative outcome (“-ㄹ 거예요”, “-겠다”, “-게 되다”), and the form “-었다가는” (“그런 말을 했다가는”) looks at what would follow if it were done. In the shifting use, the second action is something that actually happened and the subject is the same. Positive results do not take it.

examples.ko: 이렇게 매일 밤을 새우다가는 건강을 해칠 거예요.
examples.en: If you keep staying up all night like this, you will ruin your health.

examples.ko: 이러다가는 늦겠어. 빨리 가자.
examples.en: At this rate we'll be late. Let's hurry.

examples.ko: 그런 식으로 말하다가는 사람들에게 오해를 사기 쉽다.
examples.en: If you keep talking that way, you are likely to be misunderstood.

examples.ko: 온실가스 배출이 계속 늘다가는 해수면이 크게 상승할 것으로 전망된다.
examples.en: If greenhouse gas emissions keep rising, sea levels are forecast to rise sharply.

examples.ko: 민준이는 한참 창밖을 바라보다가는 갑자기 일어나 나가 버렸다.
examples.en: Minjun gazed out the window for a while and then suddenly got up and left.

compare.difference: “-다가” just reports a switch or an interruption; “-다가는” warns of a bad result.

pair.ko: 밤새 게임을 하다가는 시험을 망칠 거야.
pair.en: If you keep gaming all night, you'll ruin the exam.
I was gaming all night and ruined the exam.

compare.difference: “-으면” is a plain condition; “-다가는” takes an action already under way and warns of where it leads.

pair.en: If you keep playing like this, you'll fail the exam.
If you play like this, you'll fail the exam.

pitfalls.note: In the warning use the outcome must be bad; a good outcome takes “-으면”.
pitfalls.en: If you study hard, you will pass.

topik_tip: A “-다가는 … -ㄹ 거예요/-게 된다” sentence warns of a bad result; look for a negative outcome in the clause that follows.

label: even if, however
meaning_en: A formal connective ending for a concession: “even if X, still Y”. It grants a situation, real or assumed, and says the main clause holds regardless.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-을지라도” (“-ㄹ지라도” after a vowel or ㄹ), to nouns as “일지라도”, and after “-었-”. Adverbs such as “비록”, “아무리”, “설령” often come before it. The main clause is typically a will, advice, an order or a general truth that does not change. It is formal or literary rather than casual.

examples.ko: 아무리 힘들지라도 포기하지 마세요.
examples.en: No matter how hard it gets, please don't give up.

examples.ko: 비록 가진 것은 적을지라도 마음만은 넉넉한 사람이 되고 싶다.
examples.en: Even if I have little, I want to be a person with a generous heart.

examples.ko: 내일 세상이 끝날지라도 나는 오늘 한 그루의 사과나무를 심겠다.
examples.en: Even if the world ends tomorrow, I will plant one apple tree today.

examples.ko: 결과가 실패로 끝났을지라도 그 과정에서 배운 것은 값지다.
examples.en: Even if the result ended in failure, what was learned along the way is valuable.

examples.ko: 비록 작은 도움일지라도 정성이 담겨 있으면 큰 힘이 된다.
examples.en: Even a small help becomes a great strength when sincerity is in it.

compare.difference: “-아도/어도” is the everyday “even if”; “-을지라도” is more formal and often takes “비록” or “아무리”.

pair.en: Even if it rains, I will go.
Even if it rains, I'll go.

compare.difference: Both are concessive. “-더라도” is common in speech; “-을지라도” sounds more formal and written.

pair.en: Even if it's hard, try to the end.
Even if it is hard, please try to the end.

pitfalls.note: The main clause must run against what the first clause suggests, not simply follow from it.
pitfalls.en: If you study hard, you will pass the exam.

topik_tip: It is often found with “비록”, “아무리” or “설령”; the clause that follows usually states what stays true all the same.

label: rather than doing, better
meaning_en: A connective ending for preference: “rather than do X (which I dislike), I would do Y”. The first action is rejected, and the second is the better option.
usage: It attaches to verb stems, with no tense; a ㄹ-stem drops ㄹ (“살다 → 사느니”). The main clause states the speaker's preference, often with “차라리” and “-는 편이 낫다”, “-는 게 낫다” or a will such as “-겠다”. The repeated “-느니 -느니 하다” (“going on about doing this and that”) is a different row. The pair “-느니 … -고 말지” is a common set expression.

examples.ko: 이렇게 눈치 보며 사느니 차라리 혼자 사는 게 낫겠다.
examples.en: Rather than live like this, watching other people's moods, I'd be better off living alone.

examples.ko: 그 사람 밑에서 일하느니 차라리 그만두겠어요.
examples.en: Rather than work under that person, I'd quit.

examples.ko: 늦게 가서 욕먹느니 일찍 가서 기다리는 편이 낫다.
examples.en: It is better to go early and wait than to go late and get scolded.

examples.ko: 비싼 돈 주고 후회하느니 좀 더 알아보고 사겠습니다.
examples.en: Rather than pay a lot and regret it, I will look into it a bit more before buying.

examples.ko: 남에게 폐를 끼치느니 내가 조금 불편하고 말지.
examples.en: Rather than burden others, I'd just put up with a little inconvenience myself.

compare.difference: “-기보다는” is a plain comparison; “-느니” also rejects the first option with feeling.

pair.en: Rather than owe a friend a favour, I would walk.

pair.ko: 친구에게 신세를 지기보다 걸어가는 편이 낫다.
pair.en: Walking is better than owing a friend a favour.

compare.difference: Both mean “if it comes to this, rather”. “-을 바에는” is built on a supposed situation; “-느니” sets two options side by side.

pair.en: Rather than do it like this, I won't do it.
If I have to do it like this, I'd rather not.

pitfalls.note: It takes no past tense.
pitfalls.wrong: 그 사람을 만났느니 차라리 혼자 있겠다.
pitfalls.right: 그 사람을 만나느니 차라리 혼자 있겠다.
pitfalls.en: Rather than meet that person, I'd stay alone.

topik_tip: In 읽기 the second action after “-느니 (차라리)” is the one the speaker prefers.

label: noticing something, exclamation
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending that voices something the speaker has just noticed or realised, often with a note of surprise or admiration: “oh, look, so it is…”. The polite form is “-네요”.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems, to “이다” (“-이네”), and after “-었-” and “-겠-”; the verb needs no “-는-”. The speaker must have just noticed the fact, so it is odd for things the speaker has long known, such as one's own name or job. It is informal; the polite form is “-네요”. A different “-네” is the old-fashioned plain statement of the “하게” style (“먼저 가네”).

examples.ko: 와, 눈이 많이 왔네!
examples.en: Wow, it snowed a lot!

examples.ko: 벌써 열 시네. 이제 자야겠다.
examples.en: It's already ten o'clock. I'd better get to bed.

examples.ko: 생각보다 훨씬 어렵네.
examples.en: It's harder than I thought.

examples.ko: 어, 비가 그쳤네. 우산 안 써도 되겠다.
examples.en: Oh, the rain has stopped. I don't need the umbrella.

examples.ko: 글씨를 참 잘 쓰시네요.
examples.en: You write so beautifully.

compare.difference: “-네” voices what the speaker has just noticed; “-더라” relays something noticed earlier.

pair.en: This movie is good (I'm finding).
That movie was good (I found).

pitfalls.note: A fact the speaker already knows well cannot be voiced as a fresh discovery.
pitfalls.en: I am a student.

label: surprise, how could it be
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending for reacting to something unexpected, with surprise, disbelief or admiration: “to think that…, you mean…?!”. It often repeats back what was just said or seen.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems (“가다니”, “예쁘다니”), after “-었-” and “-겠-”, and to “이다” as “-이라니”. The imperative echo is “-으라니”. The ending alone is informal (“반말”); adding “요” gives the polite “-다니요”. The clause that follows (“믿을 수 없다”, “말도 안 돼”) often states the reaction. It can express admiration as well as shock.

examples.ko: 벌써 가다니? 아직 해도 안 졌는데.
examples.en: You're leaving already? The sun hasn't even set.

examples.ko: 이렇게 큰 선물을 주시다니 정말 감사합니다.
examples.en: To think you would give me such a big present—thank you so much.

examples.ko: 그 사람이 그런 말을 하다니 믿을 수가 없어.
examples.en: I can't believe that person would say such a thing.

examples.ko: 그 어려운 시험에 한 번에 붙다니 정말 대단하다.
examples.en: To pass such a hard exam on the first try is truly impressive.

examples.ko: 일주일 만에 책을 열 권이나 읽었다니요?
examples.en: You read as many as ten books in one week?

compare.difference: “-다고?” asks the listener to confirm what was said; “-다니” voices the speaker's own astonishment at the fact.

pair.en: Did you say you're leaving already?
Leaving already?!

compare.difference: “-네” just states a new discovery; “-다니” adds disbelief or shock.

pair.en: Oh, you're leaving already.
To think you're leaving already.

pitfalls.note: The informal ending needs “요” when speaking to someone you address politely.
pitfalls.en: Professor, you're leaving already?

pitfalls.note: After a noun, “이다” appears as “-이라니”, not “-이다니”.
pitfalls.en: I can't believe that person is a teacher.

label: doubting question: going to...?
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending that questions someone's plan or action with doubt or disapproval: “are you really going to…?”. It is a rhetorical, often critical question with rising intonation.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-으려고”, or “-려고” after a vowel or ㄹ (“가려고”, “먹으려고”). It is informal (“반말”), and the polite form is “-려고요”. It usually reacts to what the listener is doing or about to do, and it can express surprise at an unreasonable plan. The same “-려고요” can also, in a reply, state a plan (“은행에 가려고요”), which is a different use.

examples.ko: 벌써 집에 가려고? 아직 일곱 시밖에 안 됐는데.
examples.en: You're going home already? It's only seven o'clock.

examples.ko: 이렇게 많은 걸 혼자 다 먹으려고?
examples.en: You're going to eat all of this by yourself?

examples.ko: 그걸로 뭘 하려고?
examples.en: What are you going to do with that?

examples.ko: 그 옷을 입고 나가려고요? 밖이 영하인데요.
examples.en: You're going out in that? It's below zero outside.

examples.ko: 시험 전날에 놀러 가려고?
examples.en: You're going out to have fun the day before the exam?

compare.difference: The connective “-으려고” gives a purpose inside a longer sentence; the sentence-final one doubts a plan.

pair.en: I hurried in order to leave early.
You're going to leave early?

compare.difference: “-을 거야?” just asks about a plan; “-으려고?” also questions whether it is wise.

pair.en: Are you going to eat it all by yourself?
You're going to eat it all by yourself?!

pitfalls.note: After a vowel or ㄹ the ending is “-려고”, with no “으”.
pitfalls.en: You're leaving already?

label: command to a younger person
meaning_en: A command ending of the lowest speech level, used by an elder or someone in authority to a child or a younger person. It sounds affectionate, a little old-fashioned, and is common in fiction and in blessings.
usage: It attaches to verb stems and gives the command that “-아라/-어라” also gives; it is especially common after “가다” and “자다”, “있다”, “먹다”. A verb in ㄹ drops it (“살거라”). “오다” takes “-너라” (“오너라”), and with “하다” the command is “해라” or “하여라”. It is used by someone senior to someone junior, and it cannot be used toward a superior.

examples.ko: 날이 저물겠다. 어서 집에 가거라.
examples.en: It's getting dark. Hurry on home.

examples.ko: 오늘은 피곤할 테니 일찍 자거라.
examples.en: You must be tired today, so go to bed early.

examples.ko: 다음에 또 보자. 잘 가거라.
examples.en: See you next time. Take care on your way.

examples.ko: 어머니는 “밥 굶지 말고 꼭 챙겨 먹거라.” 하고 말씀하셨다.
examples.en: My mother said, “Don't skip meals; be sure to eat properly.”

examples.ko: 할머니는 손주에게 “정직하게 살거라.” 하고 당부하셨다.
examples.en: Grandmother urged her grandchild, “Live honestly.”

compare.difference: “-아라/-어라” is the ordinary plain command; “-거라” is warmer and older-sounding.

pair.en: Go to bed early (said warmly by an elder).
Go to bed early.

compare.difference: “-으렴” is a gentle, coaxing command; “-거라” is a firmer one.

pair.en: Eat a lot.
Eat plenty, dear.

pitfalls.note: For “오다” the standard command is “오너라”.
pitfalls.en: Come here.

pitfalls.note: It is for speaking down; it cannot be used to a superior.
pitfalls.en: Teacher, please go ahead.

label: of course! emphatic agreement
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending for strong agreement or confirmation: “of course, certainly, definitely”. It answers a question or backs up what the other person said.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems, to “이다” (“-이고말고”), and after “-었-”; the polite form is “-고말고요”. It is written without a space. It answers a question with a firm yes, so the answer repeats the verb or adjective of the question (“가고말고”). It is warm and emphatic, a little old-fashioned, so it is not used for a refusal.

examples.ko: “내일 모임에 올 거지?” “가고말고. 내가 빠질 수 있나.”
examples.en: “You'll come to the meeting tomorrow, right?” “Of course I will. How could I miss it?”

examples.ko: 힘들고말고. 하루 종일 서서 일했으니까.
examples.en: Of course it's hard. I worked standing up all day.

examples.ko: 그분은 정말 훌륭한 선생님이고말고요.
examples.en: That person is absolutely a wonderful teacher.

examples.ko: “도와줄 수 있어?” “도와주고말고. 걱정하지 마.”
examples.en: “Can you help me?” “Of course I can. Don't worry.”

examples.ko: 이해하고말고요. 얼마나 힘드셨겠어요.
examples.en: Of course I understand. How hard it must have been for you.

compare.difference: “-지요” agrees mildly; “-고말고요” agrees with emphasis.

pair.en: Of course it's good!
Yes, it's good.

compare.difference: “-고말고” is an emphatic yes; “-고 말다” says that something ends up happening.

pair.en: Of course I'll win.
In the end I won.

pitfalls.note: It is written together, with no space.
pitfalls.en: Of course I will go.

pitfalls.note: After a noun it needs “이다”.
pitfalls.en: That person is certainly a teacher.

label: question: do/is...?
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending for a plain question about a present fact, used in the old “하게” style and, above all, in writing for self-questions and rhetorical questions: “is it so? what is it?”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-는가”, to adjective stems as “-ㄴ가/-은가” (“큰가”, “좋은가”), to “이다” as “인가”, and “있다/없다” as “있는가”. Past is “-었는가” and future “-겠는가”. In speech it is the “하게” style of an elder to someone younger or equal, and in print it asks the reader an essay question (“…란 무엇인가?”). It is not polite to a superior.

examples.ko: 자네 요즘 어떻게 지내는가?
examples.en: How have you been these days, my friend?

examples.ko: 우리는 무엇을 위해 일하는가?
examples.en: What do we work for?

examples.ko: 진정한 행복이란 무엇인가?
examples.en: What is true happiness?

examples.ko: 이 문제의 책임은 과연 누구에게 있는가?
examples.en: Who really bears the responsibility for this problem?

examples.ko: 자네 몸은 좀 괜찮은가?
examples.en: Are you feeling a bit better?

compare.difference: “-나요” is the polite question of everyday speech; “-는가” is plain or literary.

pair.en: Is this the right way?
Is this the right way?

compare.difference: “-니” is a friendly plain question to a child or a close friend; “-는가” is the “하게” style or a written question.

pair.en: Have you eaten?
Have you eaten?

pitfalls.note: An adjective takes “-은가/-ㄴ가”, not “-는가”.
pitfalls.en: Is the weather good?

pitfalls.note: It is not a polite question to a teacher or a stranger.
pitfalls.en: Teacher, have you eaten?

topik_tip: In 읽기 essays a title or opening such as “…란 무엇인가?” is a question the rest of the passage answers.

label: oh, I see; but actually
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending with two uses. It voices a fact the speaker has just noticed, with admiration or surprise (“oh, it's quite…”), or it gives a soft objection or explanation, as in “but I actually…”. The polite form is “-는걸요”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-는걸”, to adjective stems as “-ㄴ걸/-은걸”, to “이다” as “-인걸”, and after “-었-” and “-겠-”. The polite form adds “요”. In the first use it is a discovery, much like “-네”; in the second it gently contradicts or explains (“나는 몰랐는걸”). Without “요” it is informal and not for elders.

examples.ko: 와, 이 영화 정말 재미있는걸.
examples.en: Wow, this movie is really good.

examples.ko: 생각보다 길이 많이 막히는걸.
examples.en: The roads are more jammed than I thought.

examples.ko: “왜 안 나왔어?” “나는 그 약속을 몰랐는걸.”
examples.en: “Why didn't you show up?” “But I didn't know about that appointment.”

examples.ko: 벌써 열두 시인걸요. 이제 그만 가야겠어요.
examples.en: It's already twelve o'clock. I really should go now.

examples.ko: 그 사람 노래를 진짜 잘하는걸요.
examples.en: That person really sings well!

compare.difference: “-는걸” reacts to a fact in front of you; “-을걸” is a guess about what is likely.

pair.en: Oh, it's snowing!
It will probably snow.

compare.difference: “-거든” offers a reason as background; “-는걸” gently objects or explains with a hint of surprise.

pair.en: I didn't know about that appointment, you see.
But I didn't know about that appointment.

pitfalls.note: An adjective takes “-ㄴ걸/-은걸”.
pitfalls.en: The weather is really good.

pitfalls.note: Without “요” it is informal and does not suit an elder.
pitfalls.en: Teacher, you look really good.

label: I saw, and it was...
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending for telling what the speaker personally saw, heard or tried: “(when I saw it) it was…”. The polite form is “-데요”.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems and after “-었-”; the polite form is “-데요”. The speaker must have experienced the fact directly, and often it is told with a note of discovery. It is not the “-대” that reports what someone said: “비가 오데” is what I saw, “비가 온대” is what I heard. It is also used as a question, “-데?”, which asks what the listener experienced.

examples.ko: 그 가수 노래를 직접 들어 보니 정말 잘하데.
examples.en: I heard that singer live, and they really sing well.

examples.ko: 그 집 음식은 먹어 보니 생각보다 짜데.
examples.en: I tried the food there, and it was saltier than I thought.

examples.ko: 거기 가 보니까 벌써 벚꽃이 피었데요.
examples.en: I went there, and the cherry blossoms were already out.

examples.ko: 어제 그 가게에 가 봤는데 사람이 정말 많데요.
examples.en: I went to that shop yesterday, and it was really crowded.

examples.ko: 그 사람 만나 보니 뭐라고 하데?
examples.en: You met that person; what did they say?

compare.difference: “-데” is what I experienced myself; “-대” is what I heard from someone else.

pair.en: I went there, and it was raining.
They say it is raining there.

compare.difference: “-더라고” is the more common colloquial way to report a discovery; “-데(요)” is softer and less frequent.

pair.en: The food there was salty.
The food there was salty, I found.

pitfalls.note: Do not use “-데” for what someone merely told you; that is “-대”.
pitfalls.en: According to a friend, it will rain tomorrow.

label: I found that; telling what I saw
meaning_en: A sentence-final expression for telling the listener something the speaker found out through an earlier experience: “I found that…, it turned out that…”. The polite form is “-더라고요”.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems, to “이다” (“이더라고”), and after “-었-”. It reports what the speaker saw, heard or felt in the past, mostly about someone else or a thing; for the speaker's own deliberate actions it is odd. It is conversational, and the polite form adds “요”. The adverbs “알고 보니” and “가 보니까” often go with it.

examples.ko: 어제 가 보니까 그 가게 문을 닫았더라고.
examples.en: I went by yesterday, and that shop was closed.

examples.ko: 아까 보니까 지수가 도서관에서 공부하고 있더라고요.
examples.en: I saw earlier that Jisu was studying in the library.

examples.ko: 한국 겨울이 생각보다 훨씬 춥더라고.
examples.en: Korean winters turned out to be much colder than I thought.

examples.ko: 그 책을 읽어 봤는데 내용이 어렵더라고요.
examples.en: I tried reading that book, and the content was hard.

examples.ko: 알고 보니 그 친구가 우리 학교 선배더라고.
examples.en: It turned out that friend was a senior at our school.

compare.difference: “-더라” is a flat report to oneself or a friend; “-더라고” sounds like telling the listener, and it can take “요”.

pair.en: That movie was really good.
That movie was really good, I'm telling you.

compare.difference: “-더라고” just reports; “-던데” adds background and invites a response.

pair.en: That movie was good.
That movie was good, you know (so you might watch it).

pitfalls.note: It reports something noticed, not something the speaker decided to do.
pitfalls.en: I watched a movie yesterday.

label: hearing that, I feel or judge
meaning_en: A connective expression, a contraction of “-는다고 하니”: it picks up what someone else has said and then states the speaker's reaction or judgement: “hearing that X, I am surprised, glad, or conclude that…”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-ㄴ다니/-는다니”, to adjective stems and past forms as “-다니” (“좋다니”, “갔다니”), and to “이다” as “-라니” (“학생이라니”). The same set quotes a command as “-으라니” and a suggestion as “-자니”. What follows is the speaker's feeling, evaluation or conclusion, not a plain report. It is conversational, with a sentence-final cousin that is a separate row.

examples.ko: 네가 집안일을 도와준다니 한결 마음이 놓이는구나.
examples.en: Now that you say you will help with the housework, I feel much more at ease.

examples.ko: 딸이 장학금을 받는다니 정말 기쁘시겠어요.
examples.en: Hearing that your daughter is getting a scholarship, you must be so happy.

examples.ko: 이 날씨에 소풍을 간다니 말도 안 돼.
examples.en: Going on a picnic in this weather—that's absurd.

examples.ko: 그렇게 큰 회사가 문을 닫는다니 믿기지 않는다.
examples.en: It is hard to believe that such a big company is closing down.

examples.ko: 선생님이 내일 갑자기 시험을 보라니 다들 당황했다.
examples.en: When the teacher told us we would suddenly have an exam tomorrow, everyone was flustered.

compare.difference: The sentence-final “-다니” is an exclamation of surprise; the mid-sentence “-는다니” goes on to say what that news makes the speaker feel or conclude.

pair.en: Going on a picnic?!
Going on a picnic—that is absurd.

compare.difference: “-는다니” gives the speaker's reaction to what was heard; “-는다기에” gives what was heard as the reason for an action.

pair.en: Now that you say you'll help, I feel at ease.
You said you would help, so I asked.

pitfalls.note: After a noun the ending is “-라니”, not a verb ending.
pitfalls.en: I was surprised that Minsu is a student.

label: that was, remembered past
meaning_en: A past modifier that recalls an event or state from the past and sets it apart from now: “the X that I/we did, that was, once…”. It is the “-던” of remembering added to the past “-었-”.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-았던/-었던/-였던” and to “이다” as “-이었던/-였던”, and it modifies the noun that follows (“살았던 동네”). It is used for a past period that is over, often with a feeling of looking back. It also forms “-었던 것 같다” and “-었던 적”. The plain past modifier “-은/-ㄴ” only states that something was done.

examples.ko: 아버지가 젊었던 시절의 사진을 보면 굉장히 미남이셨다.
examples.en: In photos from the days when my father was young, he was strikingly handsome.

examples.ko: 우리가 처음 만났던 카페는 이제 문을 닫았다.
examples.en: The cafe where we first met has closed now.

examples.ko: 어릴 때 살았던 동네에 오랜만에 가 봤다.
examples.en: I visited, after a long time, the neighborhood where I lived as a child.

examples.ko: 지금 생각해 보면 그때 나는 너무 어렸던 것 같다.
examples.en: Thinking about it now, I seem to have been too young then.

examples.ko: 학생이었던 그 사람이 이제는 선생님이 되었다.
examples.en: That person who was a student has now become a teacher.

compare.difference: “-ㄴ” merely says an action was completed; “-었던” recalls it as part of a past that is over.

pair.en: The bibimbap I ate yesterday was good.
The bibimbap I ate as a child was good (I remember).

compare.difference: “-던” looks back at an action that was in progress or habitual; “-었던” looks back at a finished stretch.

pair.en: The house I used to live in was very small.
The house where I once lived was very small.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel the form is “-이었던” or the contraction “-였던”, not “-이였던”.
pitfalls.en: A person who was a student became a teacher.

label: about, concerning
meaning_en: A formal expression meaning “about, concerning”: it names the subject matter of what follows. “에 관한” modifies a noun, and “에 관해서” is the spoken variant.
usage: It attaches to nouns. “에 관하여” (or “에 관해(서)”) works as an adverb before a verb, and “에 관한” works as a modifier before a noun (“날씨에 관한 속담”). It states what a talk, text or study is about, not the direction of a feeling toward something. It is formal and common in writing, and “에 관해서는” can mark a topic.

examples.ko: 우리나라에는 날씨에 관한 속담이 많다.
examples.en: In Korea there are many proverbs about the weather.

examples.ko: 이 문제에 관하여 여러분의 의견을 듣고 싶습니다.
examples.en: I would like to hear your opinions about this issue.

examples.ko: 한국의 전통문화에 관한 책을 한 권 샀다.
examples.en: I bought a book about traditional Korean culture.

examples.ko: 사건에 관하여 경찰은 아직 아무런 입장을 밝히지 않았다.
examples.en: The police have not yet stated any position on the case.

examples.ko: 민준이는 이 일에 관해서는 아무 말도 하지 않았다.
examples.en: Minjun said nothing about this matter.

compare.difference: “에 대하여” also covers an attitude or feeling directed at something; “에 관하여” only names the subject matter.

pair.en: I read a book about the environment.
Interest in the environment has risen.

compare.difference: “와 관련하여” says something is connected to the topic; “에 관하여” says it is about the topic.

pair.en: I saw the news about the traffic accident.
I saw the news related to the traffic accident.

pitfalls.note: It names a subject matter, so it does not fit a feeling aimed at someone.
pitfalls.en: My love for my parents is deep.

pitfalls.note: Before a noun use the modifier “에 관한”, not “에 관하여”.
pitfalls.en: There are many proverbs about the weather.

label: since someone suggested
meaning_en: A connective expression, a contraction of “-자고 하기에”: it presents a suggestion someone made as the reason for what the speaker (or another person) then did.
usage: It attaches to verb stems only, quoting a “let's…” suggestion. The main clause tells what was done in response, almost always in the past. The subject of the suggestion is someone other than the speaker. It is conversational or narrative, and it cannot lead into a command or a suggestion of the speaker's own.

examples.ko: 친구가 같이 점심을 먹자기에 식당에 갔다.
examples.en: A friend suggested we have lunch together, so I went to a restaurant.

examples.ko: 동생이 영화를 보러 가자기에 오랜만에 극장에 갔다.
examples.en: My younger sibling suggested going to see a movie, so I went to the theater for the first time in a while.

examples.ko: 승규가 주말에 등산을 가자기에 흔쾌히 승낙했다.
examples.en: Seunggyu suggested going hiking on the weekend, so I gladly agreed.

examples.ko: 유민이가 잠깐 쉬었다 가자기에 벤치에 앉았다.
examples.en: Yumin suggested resting a while before going on, so we sat down on a bench.

examples.ko: 선배가 한잔하자기에 못 이기는 척 따라갔다.
examples.en: A senior colleague suggested a drink, so I went along, pretending to give in.

compare.difference: “-자고 해서” is the plain full form of the reason; “-자기에” is its contraction and sounds quicker and more colloquial.

pair.en: A friend suggested lunch, so I went out.
A friend said let's have lunch, so I went out.

compare.difference: “-자기에” quotes a suggestion; “-는다기에” quotes a statement.

pair.en: A friend suggested seeing a movie, so I went.
A friend said they were going to see a movie, so I tagged along.

pitfalls.note: The result clause reports what was done; it cannot be a command or a suggestion.
pitfalls.en: A friend suggested eating, so I ate.

label: bound to, natural result
meaning_en: An expression for what is natural and bound to happen: “is bound to, tends to, it goes without saying that…”. It states a general truth about how things turn out.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems and is usually in the present (“-게 마련이다”); the narrative past is “-게 마련이었다”. The form “-기 마련이다” is equally correct and more common. It states a general rule or tendency, not a particular prediction. It is typical of essays and advice.

examples.ko: 거짓말은 하다 보면 점점 더 커지게 마련이다.
examples.en: Lies are bound to grow bigger as you keep telling them.

examples.ko: 사람은 누구나 실수를 하게 마련이다.
examples.en: Everyone is bound to make mistakes.

examples.ko: 노력한 만큼 결과가 나오게 마련이에요.
examples.en: Results are bound to come in proportion to the effort.

examples.ko: 시간이 지나면 아픈 기억도 흐려지게 마련이다.
examples.en: As time passes, even painful memories are bound to fade.

examples.ko: 만나면 헤어지게 마련이고 태어나면 죽게 마련이다.
examples.en: What meets must part, and what is born must die.

compare.difference: They mean the same; “-기 마련이다” is the more common form.

pair.en: People are bound to make mistakes.
People are bound to make mistakes.

compare.difference: “-는 법이다” speaks of a rule or the way the world is; “-게 마련이다” stresses that a result inevitably follows.

pair.en: When winter goes, spring comes; that is how it is.
When winter goes, spring is bound to come.

pitfalls.note: It states a general truth, so it does not suit a prediction about one particular event.
pitfalls.en: It will rain tomorrow.

topik_tip: A “-기/-게 마련이다” sentence states a universal tendency, so a clause about one specific event does not fit it.

label: going to end up in trouble
meaning_en: A colloquial expression meaning that the speaker (or someone) is about to end up in an unwelcome situation: “looks like I'm going to have to…, I'm about to end up…”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems and is always in the past form “생겼다” (“생겼네”, “생겼어요”), even though it points to the immediate future. The situation is nearly always bad or inconvenient, and it often follows a reason clause (“-아서”, “-는 바람에”). It has no positive uses. Do not confuse it with “-게 생겼다” in the sense of how someone looks (“착하게 생겼다”).

examples.ko: 쌀이 없어서 저녁을 굶게 생겼다.
examples.en: We're out of rice, so we're going to miss dinner.

examples.ko: 갑자기 비가 와서 소풍을 못 가게 생겼다.
examples.en: It suddenly started raining, so it looks like the picnic is off.

examples.ko: 이러다간 마감에 늦게 생겼어.
examples.en: At this rate I'm going to miss the deadline.

examples.ko: 이번 달 월급이 안 나와서 월세를 못 내게 생겼어요.
examples.en: My pay isn't coming this month, so I'm going to be unable to pay the rent.

examples.ko: 이번 주말에도 야근을 하게 생겼다.
examples.en: Looks like I'll be working late this weekend too.

examples.ko: 지수는 열쇠를 잃어버려서 집에 못 들어가게 생겼다.
examples.en: Jisu has lost the key, so it looks like they won't get into the house.

compare.difference: “-게 되다” says that a change happens, with no tone; “-게 생겼다” says one is on the brink of a bad situation.

pair.en: At this rate I'm going to be late.
At this rate I will end up being late.

compare.difference: The same words can describe appearance: “-게 생기다” (looks like) is a description, while “-게 생겼다” in this row is a situation.

pair.en: I'm about to end up going hungry.
That person looks kind.

pitfalls.note: It is for unwelcome situations; good news takes another form.
pitfalls.en: I think I'll win the lottery.

label: depends on how you do it
meaning_en: An expression meaning that the result depends on how one does the action: “it all depends on how you…, it's up to…”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-기 나름이다” (“생각하기 나름”), with no tense before “-기”. It is used with verbs of thinking, doing and handling (“마음먹기”, “하기”, “쓰기”). The result clause is usually a general claim about what differs. The related “-기에 따라” means the same, but takes “달라지다” as its predicate.

examples.ko: 행복은 마음먹기 나름이에요.
examples.en: Happiness depends on how you set your mind.

examples.ko: 아이의 습관은 부모가 가르치기 나름이다.
examples.en: A child's habits depend on how the parents teach.

examples.ko: 그 일이 쉬운지 어려운지는 하기 나름이야.
examples.en: Whether that job is easy or hard depends on how you do it.

examples.ko: 성적은 노력하기 나름이니 아직 포기하지 마.
examples.en: Grades depend on how much effort you put in, so don't give up yet.

examples.ko: 인생은 살아가기 나름이라고들 한다.
examples.en: They say life depends on how you live it.

compare.difference: “-기 나름이다” ends the sentence with the claim; “-기에 따라” leads into a result that differs.

pair.en: The taste depends on how you make it.
The taste varies depending on how you make it.

compare.difference: “에 달려 있다” points to a person or a thing as the deciding factor; “-기 나름이다” points to the manner of doing.

pair.en: The result depends on how you try.
The result depends on effort.

pitfalls.note: The verb before “-기” takes no tense.
pitfalls.en: It depends on how hard you try.

pitfalls.note: It uses the noun form “-기”, not the adnominal “-는”.
pitfalls.en: It depends on how you try.

label: as soon as, no sooner than
meaning_en: An expression meaning “as soon as, no sooner had X than Y”: the second action follows the first at once, often with a sense of haste.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-기가 바쁘게”, with no tense before “-기”. The main clause is in the past, because it reports what followed immediately; it cannot be a command or a suggestion. The subjects of the two clauses can differ. It is more vivid than “-자마자”, and the synonym “-기가 무섭게” is a separate form. It is colloquial and narrative.

examples.ko: 민준이는 점심시간 종이 울리기가 바쁘게 식당으로 달려갔다.
examples.en: No sooner had the lunch bell rung than Minjun ran to the cafeteria.

examples.ko: 회의가 끝나기가 바쁘게 모두 자리를 떠났다.
examples.en: As soon as the meeting ended, everyone left their seats.

examples.ko: 문이 열리기가 바쁘게 사람들이 뛰어 들어갔다.
examples.en: The doors had barely opened when people rushed in.

examples.ko: 영수는 월급을 받기가 바쁘게 다 써 버렸다.
examples.en: Yeongsu spent it all the moment they were paid.

examples.ko: 퇴근 시간이 되기가 바쁘게 직원들은 사무실을 나섰다.
examples.en: As soon as it was closing time, the staff left the office.

compare.difference: “-자마자” is neutral; “-기가 바쁘게” adds a feeling of rush and is used mainly in narration.

pair.en: I fell asleep as soon as I got home.
I fell asleep the instant I got home.

compare.difference: “-는 대로” can look to the future; “-기가 바쁘게” only reports something that already happened.

pair.en: I'll call you as soon as I arrive.
I called the moment I arrived.

pitfalls.note: It reports something already done, so it cannot lead into a command.
pitfalls.en: Please call as soon as you arrive.

label: is apt to, likely to
meaning_en: An expression meaning that something is likely to happen or that one is apt to do it: “it is easy to end up…, is apt to…”. It usually warns of an undesirable tendency.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems, with the “가” often dropped (“-기 쉽다”), and with no tense before “-기”. It describes a general tendency, often a risk (“걸리기 쉽다”, “깨지기 쉽다”). It is not a prediction about one specific event. The colloquial synonym “-기 십상이다” is another form, stronger and always negative.

examples.ko: 환절기에는 감기에 걸리기가 쉽다.
examples.en: In the change of seasons it is easy to catch a cold.

examples.ko: 이 유리잔은 깨지기가 쉬우니 조심해서 다루세요.
examples.en: This glass breaks easily, so please handle it carefully.

examples.ko: 급하게 결정하면 실수하기가 쉽다.
examples.en: If you decide in a hurry, you are apt to make mistakes.

examples.ko: 아이들은 인터넷에서 잘못된 정보를 믿기가 쉽다.
examples.en: Children are apt to believe wrong information on the internet.

examples.ko: 사람은 자기 입장에서만 생각하기가 쉬워서 오해가 생긴다.
examples.en: People easily think only from their own standpoint, so misunderstandings arise.

compare.difference: “-기 십상이다” is the stronger, colloquial form and is always about a bad result.

pair.en: If you hurry, you are apt to make mistakes.
If you hurry, you are almost sure to make mistakes.

compare.difference: “-을 수 있다” says something is possible; “-기 쉽다” says it tends to happen.

pair.en: You may catch a cold.
You are apt to catch a cold.

pitfalls.note: The tense does not go before “-기”.
pitfalls.en: You are apt to catch a cold.

pitfalls.note: It describes a general tendency, so it does not suit a forecast for one day.
pitfalls.en: It is very likely to rain tomorrow.

label: only does, just keeps being
meaning_en: An expression meaning that one does only that one thing and nothing else, or, with an adjective, that a state simply stays as it is: “do nothing but, only, is just…”.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-기만 하다”; the tense goes on “하다” (“웃기만 했다”), never before “-기”. With a verb, it says nothing else is done (“듣기만 하다”), and with an adjective, it says the state does not change (“어렵기만 하다”). “-기만 하지 말고” (“don't just…”) is a common set phrase. The related “-기만 하면” is a different pattern.

examples.ko: 승규는 묻는 말에는 대답하지 않고 웃기만 했다.
examples.en: Seunggyu did not answer the question and only smiled.

examples.ko: 휴일에는 집에서 먹고 자기만 한다.
examples.en: On holidays all I do at home is eat and sleep.

examples.ko: 새 학교는 아직 낯설기만 해요.
examples.en: The new school is still just strange to me.

examples.ko: 걱정하기만 하지 말고 일단 시작해 봐.
examples.en: Don't just worry; start first.

examples.ko: 어머니는 말없이 듣기만 하시고 아무 말씀도 하지 않으셨다.
examples.en: My mother only listened in silence and said nothing.

compare.difference: They are close in meaning; “-을 뿐이다” is the more formal and literary.

pair.en: The child did nothing but cry.
The child could do nothing but cry.

compare.difference: “-기만 하다” says nothing else is done; “-고만 있다” stresses that a single action simply goes on.

pair.en: The child did nothing but cry.
The child kept on crying.

pitfalls.note: The tense goes on “하다”, not before “-기”.
pitfalls.en: I only smiled.
